title: Fatimah and Ali
hookLine: the Prophet's daughter Fatimah marries Ali, and the bride price is a coat of armor (Abu Dawud)

lines: A YOUNG MAN WITH ALMOST NOTHING.
cards: A young man wants to marry, and he has almost nothing. That's Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. The woman is Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
Ali asks for her hand, and the Prophet asks him: what will you give her? Ali says he has nothing. And the Prophet, who knows him well, asks a very practical question: where is your armor?
Not a poem. Not a promise. Today: mahr.

teach.h: THE MAHR WAS A COAT OF ARMOR.
teach.b: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Abbas. Ali says he has nothing to give, the Prophet reminds him of his coat of armor, and that armor becomes the mahr, the bride's gift.
In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride, not to her father.

teach.h: A CLOTH, A WATER SKIN, A PILLOW.
teach.b: A report in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i lists what the Prophet gave Fatimah for the new home: a cloth, a water skin, and a leather pillow stuffed with a fragrant grass. That's the whole list.
Set beside it his advice to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market.

teach.h: A MEAL, EVEN WITH ONE SHEEP.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, when Abd al-Rahman married, the Prophet told him to hold a wedding meal, even if only with one sheep. The meal mattered. The size didn't.
Bukhari tells of a day the Prophet came to Fatimah's house and Ali wasn't there. She said there had been something between them, and he had gone out angry.

The Prophet found him asleep in the mosque, his cloak slipped off, his side covered in dust, and began brushing it off him: get up, Abu Turab. Father of dust. Ali, the report says, loved that name more than any other.
A small quarrel, and a father-in-law who came with a joke instead of a lecture. In Bukhari too, the Prophet says: Fatimah is a part of me.
Sunni and Shi'a tradition both honor Fatimah and Ali, and this is where their household began: with very little, and with love.

how: Muslim weddings vary widely by culture, but the mahr given to the bride and a walimah, a wedding meal, are part of the practice, and some couples keep both deliberately modest, remembering Fatimah and Ali.

o: the dowry a bride's family brings to the marriage
the gift a groom gives that belongs to the bride

s: Ali came to the marriage with plenty to give
he said he had nothing, and the Prophet reminded him of his armor (Abu Dawud).
Abu Turab, father of dust, began as a gentle joke

games.q: your son-in-law has walked out after a quarrel with your daughter. you find him asleep in the mosque, covered in dust. what do you do?
o: wake him and tell him to go home and apologize.
brush the dust off him and call him father of dust.
leave him there and go back to your daughter.
games.why: in Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ brushed the dust off Ali and said: get up, Abu Turab. Ali loved that name.

practice: Think of something coming up that you're meant to mark, a birthday, an anniversary, a small win, and notice what the plans cost, in money and in worry.
Then ask what the armor is: the one thing that actually matters, a meal together, a word said out loud, the right people in the room.
If you pray, you can ask Allah for blessing on the people you'll celebrate with; if not, just hold their faces in mind.

wordCard.voice: Mahr, the bride's gift. Fatimah and Ali married with a coat of armor for hers, and a home of very few things. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the Prophet's daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.

carryVoice: Your line: a simple wedding. The gift was armor, and the home held three things. See you tomorrow.
